My point estimates were anchored primarily to the assumption that the asset was trading near 1020 at the time of the forecast, with modest upward drift built in at each horizon. For the one-day estimate of 1021.5, I essentially assumed near-term mean reversion and low overnight volatility, projecting only a marginal move from the prevailing price. The one-week estimate of 1025 incorporated a slight positive drift assumption, consistent with modest bullish momentum or a mild risk-on environment, while the one-month estimate of 1035 extended that drift further, reflecting the idea that over longer horizons small systematic biases tend to accumulate. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively close together, signaling that I did not expect any dramatic directional catalyst in the near term.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 23 points reflects normal intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to plus or minus 50 points, capturing the possibility of meaningful macro data releases, central bank commentary, or shifts in sentiment over five trading sessions. At one month, the interval stretches to plus or minus 95 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, cumulative news flow, earnings, geopolitical developments, and liquidity conditions can all move markets substantially. This progressive widening is consistent with how realized volatility typically scales with the square root of time, though I allowed for somewhat fatter tails than a pure Gaussian model would suggest.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside even the stated 90% intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock such as an unexpected central bank rate decision, a deterioration in credit conditions, or a geopolitical escalation could produce a sharp selloff that breaks through the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data print, a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical risk, or a short-squeeze dynamic could send prices well above the upper bounds. Liquidity events, such as a flash crash or a large forced seller entering the market, represent tail risks that are difficult to quantify but are real possibilities.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that these estimates are only as good as the assumptions embedded in them.
